The signal in embedded data is low-dimensional, explaining why distributional shifts are easily detectable.
papers.limitation: For short text samples (e.g., one sentence), it is difficult to distinguish between human and machine translations.
papers.abstract: Constructing high-quality features is critical to any quantitative data analysis. While feature engineering was historically addressed by carefully hand-crafting data representations based on domain expertise, deep neural networks (DNNs) now offer a radically different approach. DNNs implicitly engineer features by transforming their input data into hidden feature vectors called embeddings. For embedding vectors produced by foundation models -- which are trained to be useful across many contexts -- we demonstrate that simple and well-studied dimensionality-reduction techniques such as Principal Component Analysis uncover inherent heterogeneity in input data concordant with human-understandable explanations. Of the many applications for this framework, we find empirical evidence that there is intrinsic separability between real samples and those generated by artificial intelligence (AI).

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: On the Origins of the Block Structure Phenomenon in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: What is the origin of the block structure phenomenon in neural network representations? Does it arise from overfitting to spurious data features or does it capture meaningful dataset statistics?
papers.core_contribution: The block structure phenomenon arises from dominant datapoints that share simple image statistics (e.g., background color), which vary across random seeds. The block structure can be eliminated via principal component regularization without harming performance.
papers.conclusion: The block structure captures real but simple dataset statistics, and its inconsistency across seeds is due to variation in which statistics are captured. Training interventions like principal component regularization can reduce the block structure and improve representational consistency.
papers.key_findings:
The block structure is caused by a small set of dominant datapoints that share similar image statistics (e.g., background color).
The set of dominant datapoints and the specific image statistic they capture vary across random seeds.
Removing dominant datapoints from the analysis eliminates the block structure.
The block structure emerges early in training, but the dominant datapoints and representations continue to change substantially.
Principal component regularization can eliminate the block structure and improve model consistency across seeds without hurting accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Focus on image classification tasks and ResNet architectures; it remains to be seen how the block structure manifests in other domains and architectures.
Analysis is primarily empirical; a theoretical understanding is left for future work.
future_direction: Exploring how dominant datapoints manifest in other domains and applications.
Applying principal component regularization to distribution shift and self-supervision problems.
papers.abstract: Recent work has uncovered a striking phenomenon in large-capacity neural networks: they contain blocks of contiguous hidden layers with highly similar representations. This block structure has two seemingly contradictory properties: on the one hand, its constituent layers exhibit highly similar dominant first principal components (PCs), but on the other hand, their representations, and their common first PC, are highly dissimilar across different random seeds. Our work seeks to reconcile these discrepant properties by investigating the origin of the block structure in relation to the data and training methods. By analyzing properties of the dominant PCs, we find that the block structure arises from dominant datapoints - a small group of examples that share similar image statistics (e.g. background color). However, the set of dominant datapoints, and the precise shared image statistic, can vary across random seeds. Thus, the block structure reflects meaningful dataset statistics, but is simultaneously unique to each model. Through studying hidden layer activations and creating synthetic datapoints, we demonstrate that these simple image statistics dominate the representational geometry of the layers inside the block structure. We explore how the phenomenon evolves through training, finding that the block structure takes shape early in training, but the underlying representations and the corresponding dominant datapoints continue to change substantially. Finally, we study the interplay between the block structure and different training mechanisms, introducing a targeted intervention to eliminate the block structure, as well as examining the effects of pretraining and Shake-Shake regularization.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional information into automatic circuit discovery for language models to address limitations of position-agnostic methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware circuit discovery (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, achieving better faithfulness than position-agnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: Position-aware circuit discovery and schemas improve circuit faithfulness and enable automated analysis of variable-length inputs, providing a more precise foundation for mechanistic explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Position-aware circuits are smaller and more faithful than position-agnostic circuits.
Automatically generated schemas (with or without saliency masks) yield circuits comparable to those from human-designed schemas.
The proposed method handles variable-length inputs via schemas, enabling circuit discovery in more naturalistic settings.
papers.limitation:
Schemas assume sequential order of spans, which may not hold for all datasets.
The schema generation and application pipeline may not always produce valid schemas for all examples.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
Investigate the components in the circuit for the Winobias task to understand the balance between task-relevant and bias-inducing factors.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: Explainable AI in drug discovery: self-interpretable graph neural network for molecular property prediction using concept whitening
papers.research_question: How can concept whitening be adapted to graph neural networks to create self-interpretable models for molecular property prediction in drug discovery, and does this improve both performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts the concept whitening (CW) interpretability method to graph neural networks, enabling self-interpretable QSAR models that align latent space axes with known molecular properties (concepts) and identify relevant structural parts of molecules for predictions.
papers.conclusion: The adaptation of concept whitening to graph neural networks provides an effective framework for building self-interpretable models in drug discovery, offering improved performance and clear insights into the molecular properties driving predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Adding concept whitening layers to GNNs improves classification performance (ROC-AUC) and interpretability on molecular property prediction tasks.
The method successfully identifies which predefined molecular properties (concepts) are most relevant for predictions at different network depths.
Two novel activation modes for CW in GNNs (weighted_topk_pool and topk_pool) are introduced and evaluated.
The choice of normalization layer (BatchNorm, InstanceNorm, LayerNorm, GraphNorm) in the base model affects the performance after adding CW layers.
The method provides both structural (via GNNExplainer) and conceptual explanations for model predictions in drug discovery.

papers.title: GPCR-BERT: Interpreting Sequential Design of G Protein Coupled Receptors Using Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the correlation between variations in conserved motifs of GPCRs and other amino acids? Can we predict missing residues and identify key contributing amino acids?
papers.core_contribution: Developed GPCR-BERT, a fine-tuned protein language model, to interpret sequential design of GPCRs, achieving high accuracy in predicting masked residues and identifying residue correlations through attention analysis.
papers.conclusion: GPCR-BERT effectively predicts residues and distinguishes GPCR classes, providing insights into functional relationships and potential applications in mutation studies and drug development.
papers.key_findings:
GPCR-BERT achieved high accuracy (up to 100%) in predicting masked residues in conserved motifs.
The model successfully clustered GPCRs of the same class in embedding space, indicating it captures class-specific features.
Attention analysis revealed correlations between masked residues and other amino acids, some of which align with experimental mutagenesis data.
The model's predictions for CWxP motif were less accurate, likely due to smaller dataset size.
GPCR-BERT outperformed BERT and SVM on the prediction tasks, demonstrating the advantage of protein-specific pre-training.
papers.limitation: The conserved motifs are not 100% conserved (e.g., CWxP motif is only 71% conserved), so the model might not apply to GPCRs with varied versions of the motifs.
papers.abstract: With the rise of Transformers and Large Language Models (LLMs) in Chemistry and Biology, new avenues for the design and understanding of therapeutics have opened up to the scientific community. Protein sequences can be modeled as language and can take advantage of recent advances in LLMs, specifically with the abundance of our access to the protein sequence datasets. In this paper, we developed the GPCR-BERT model for understanding the sequential design of G Protein-Coupled Receptors (GPCRs). GPCRs are the target of over one-third of FDA-approved pharmaceuticals. However, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding the relationship between amino acid sequence, ligand selectivity, and conformational motifs (such as NPxxY, CWxP, E/DRY). By utilizing the pre-trained protein model (Prot-Bert) and fine-tuning with prediction tasks of variations in the motifs, we were able to shed light on several relationships between residues in the binding pocket and some of the conserved motifs. To achieve this, we took advantage of attention weights, and hidden states of the model that are interpreted to extract the extent of contributions of amino acids in dictating the type of masked ones. The fine-tuned models demonstrated high accuracy in predicting hidden residues within the motifs. In addition, the analysis of embedding was performed over 3D structures to elucidate the higher-order interactions within the conformations of the receptors.

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks encode information in superposition, meaning multiple concepts are linearly combined in a shared representational space.
Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation.
Sparse coding methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can extract disentangled, interpretable features from superposed neural representations.
Quantitative interpretability metrics, like psychophysics tasks, are needed to assess the success of feature extraction methods.
The framework bridges insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes sparse latent variables in Euclidean space, whereas some latent variables (e.g., object pose) may have non-Euclidean topology, and the linear representation hypothesis may only hold approximately in such cases.
Practical recovery of sparse codes in large-scale models remains challenging, requiring more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms.
Interpretability scores based on pairwise human similarity judgments are insufficient as they depend on context, motivating the need for contextualized similarity metrics.
future_direction: Extending the framework to incorporate latent variables with non-Euclidean geometry or discrete structure.
Developing more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms for large-scale models.
Addressing the binding problem—how multiple objects and attributes are encoded without losing relational information when representations are summed.
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is represented in neural networks is a fundamental challenge in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Despite their nonlinear architectures, recent evidence suggests that neural networks encode features in superposition, meaning that input concepts are linearly overlaid within the network's representations. We present a perspective that explains this phenomenon and provides a foundation for extracting interpretable representations from neural activations. Our theoretical framework consists of three steps: (1) Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation. (2) Sparse coding methods can extract disentangled features from these representations by leveraging principles from compressed sensing. (3) Quantitative interpretability metrics provide a means to assess the success of these methods, ensuring that extracted features align with human-interpretable concepts. By bridging insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research, we propose an emerging perspective on understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems. Our arguments have implications for neural coding theories, AI transparency, and the broader goal of making deep learning models more interpretable.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Interpretability and Generalization Bounds for Learning Spatial Physics
papers.research_question: How does the function space of training data affect the generalization of machine learning models when learning linear differential equations, and can learned models be interpreted in terms of Green's functions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that generalization in learning spatial physics depends critically on the function space of the training data, and introduces a cross-validation technique and a mechanistic interpretability lens based on extracting Green's functions from learned models.
papers.conclusion: Learning spatially dependent problems is limited by the underlying function space of the training data, and careful data selection and cross-validation are needed; different model classes exhibit opposing generalization behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Learned parameters in finite difference models converge with error depending on grid spacing and polynomial order of data.
Linear models only converge to a projection of the true operator onto the subspace of the training data, limiting out-of-distribution generalization.
Deep models and SciML models (DeepONet, Neural Operator) do not always generalize out-of-distribution.
Physics-informed losses (PINNs, PI-DeepONet) suffer from the same subspace limitation as black-box models.
Green's function operators can be extracted from black-box models when they generalize effectively across test domains.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis requires a priori knowledge of how the dataset was constructed.
Real-world data collection has inherent limitations that may hinder discovering unknown physics.
future_direction: Develop new methods capable of discovering the underlying subspace of the data to compensate for limitations.
Use cross-set generalization as an evaluation benchmark for future differential equation learning techniques.
papers.abstract: While there are many applications of ML to scientific problems that look promising, visuals can be deceiving. Using numerical analysis techniques, we rigorously quantify the accuracy, convergence rates, and generalization bounds of certain ML models applied to linear differential equations for parameter discovery or solution finding. Beyond the quantity and discretization of data, we identify that the function space of the data is critical to the generalization of the model. A similar lack of generalization is empirically demonstrated for commonly used models, including physics-specific techniques. Counterintuitively, we find that different classes of models can exhibit opposing generalization behaviors. Based on our theoretical analysis, we also introduce a new mechanistic interpretability lens on scientific models whereby Green's function representations can be extracted from the weights of black-box models. Our results inform a new cross-validation technique for measuring generalization in physical systems, which can serve as a benchmark.

papers.title: Measuring Compositionality in Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How can we measure compositional structure in learned representations? And how does compositionality relate to learning dynamics, human judgments, representational similarity, and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Tree Reconstruction Error (TRE), a method for measuring compositional structure in learned representations, and applies it to study compositionality in relation to learning dynamics, human judgments, similarity, and generalization.
papers.conclusion: TRE provides a tool for evaluating compositionality in representation learning, opening up new directions for understanding models and the conditions that give rise to compositional representations.
papers.key_findings:
TRE tracks compositionality over learning, showing compression in the information bottleneck framework is associated with discovery of compositional representations.
TRE correlates with human judgments of compositionality for noun-noun compounds.
Compositionality (low TRE) imposes constraints on similarity between representations (Proposition 1).
In communication games, compositionality is correlated with generalization error, but low TRE is not necessary for good generalization and can sometimes indicate trivial strategies.
papers.limitation:
TRE requires oracle derivations (known compositional structure of inputs)
Low TRE can correspond to trivial strategies that yield poor overall performance
future_direction: Generalizing TRE to settings without oracle derivations (unsupervised grammar induction)
Using TRE to better understand existing machine learning models
Understanding data distributions and loss functions that give rise to compositional representations
papers.abstract: Many machine learning algorithms represent input data with vector embeddings or discrete codes. When inputs exhibit compositional structure (e.g. objects built from parts or procedures from subroutines), it is natural to ask whether this compositional structure is reflected in the the inputs' learned representations. While the assessment of compositionality in languages has received significant attention in linguistics and adjacent fields, the machine learning literature lacks general-purpose tools for producing graded measurements of compositional structure in more general (e.g. vector-valued) representation spaces. We describe a procedure for evaluating compositionality by measuring how well the true representation-producing model can be approximated by a model that explicitly composes a collection of inferred representational primitives. We use the procedure to provide formal and empirical characterizations of compositional structure in a variety of settings, exploring the relationship between compositionality and learning dynamics, human judgments, representational similarity, and generalization.

papers.title: MolReasoner: Toward Effective and Interpretable Reasoning for Molecular LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across various domains, but their ability to perform molecular reasoning remains underexplored. Existing methods mostly rely on general-purpose prompting, which lacks domain-specific molecular semantics, or fine-tuning, which faces challenges in interpretability and reasoning depth, often leading to structural and textual hallucinations. To address these issues, we introduce MolReasoner, a two-stage framework that transitions LLMs from memorization to high-fidelity chemical reasoning. In the Mol-SFT stage, knowledge-enhanced Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data provides a strong foundation, while the Mol-RL stage refines reasoning using a novel, task-adaptive reward system to mitigate hallucinations. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MolReasoner significantly outperforms a wide range of strong baselines in both molecule generation and captioning tasks. Further analyses highlight the framework's synergistic design and its ability to produce more interpretable outputs. Our work presents a principled and effective new approach for advancing high-fidelity molecular reasoning.

papers.title: DGTN: Graph-Enhanced Transformer with Diffusive Attention Gating Mechanism for Enzyme DDG Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we accurately predict the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (∆∆G) by integrating sequence and structural information through a co-learning framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DGTN, a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network and transformer representations through a bidirectional diffusion mechanism for protein stability prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: DGTN effectively integrates 3D geometric and evolutionary sequence context through bidirectional diffusion, establishing a principled and interpretable paradigm for accurate protein stability prediction and design.
papers.key_findings:
DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance on ProTherm with Pearson correlation ρ=0.87 and RMSE=1.21 kcal/mol, outperforming existing baselines.
Ablation studies show the bidirectional diffusion mechanism contributes a 6-point gain in Pearson correlation over simple cross-modal fusion.
The model generalizes well to unseen datasets (SKEMPI, Ssym, FireProtDB), demonstrating robust learning of stability principles.
Theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to an optimal structure-aware attention matrix with a convergence rate of O(1/√T).
Attention visualization confirms the model successfully identifies spatially proximate but sequentially distant residue interactions.
papers.limitation:
Operates on a single static conformation of the wild-type protein, unable to capture dynamic or entropic contributions to stability.
Evaluates mutations in isolation and does not explicitly model epistatic (non-additive) interactions between multiple substitutions.
Training data (ProTherm) exhibits class imbalance, with certain protein families overrepresented, potentially limiting generalization.
future_direction: Incorporate ensembles of structures (from molecular dynamics or predicted distributions) to model flexibility and allostery.
Extend the architecture to jointly represent combinatorial mutations via graph-based mutation encoding or interaction-aware attention.
Improve robustness to dataset imbalance via domain-adversarial training, balanced sampling, or cross-family transfer learning.
papers.abstract: Predicting the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (DDG) is fundamental to protein engineering and drug design. While recent deep learning approaches have shown promise, they often process sequence and structure information independently, failing to capture the intricate coupling between local structural geometry and global sequential patterns. We present DGTN (Diffused Graph-Transformer Network), a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network (GNN) weights for structural priors and transformer attention through a diffusion mechanism. Our key innovation is a bidirectional diffusion process where: (1) GNN-derived structural embeddings guide transformer attention via learnable diffusion kernels, and (2) transformer representations refine GNN message passing through attention-modulated graph updates. We provide rigorous mathematical analysis showing this co-learning scheme achieves provably better approximation bounds than independent processing. On ProTherm and SKEMPI benchmarks, DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance (Pearson Rho = 0.87, RMSE = 1.21 kcal/mol), with 6.2% improvement over best baselines. Ablation studies confirm the diffusion mechanism contributes 4.8 points to correlation. Our theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to optimal structure-sequence coupling, with convergence rate O(1/sqrt(T) ) where T is diffusion steps. This work establishes a principled framework for integrating heterogeneous protein representations through learnable diffusion.

papers.title: Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks
papers.research_question: Why do neural networks arrive at particular computational strategies when trained on algebraic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that margin maximization can fully specify the features learned by neural networks on algebraic tasks, explaining why networks arrive at particular computational strategies such as Fourier features for modular addition.
papers.conclusion: Margin maximization fully specifies the features learned on algebraic tasks, providing insight into why networks adopt particular computational strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Maximum margin solutions for modular addition use neurons that are sparse in Fourier space, each neuron corresponding to a single frequency.
For sparse parity, maximum margin solutions have neurons that assign equal magnitude weights to relevant bits and satisfy a sign condition.
For finite group operations, maximum margin solutions use neurons that correspond to irreducible representations of the group.
Neural networks trained with gradient descent and small regularization approach the maximum margin solution, and their learned features match the theoretical predictions.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to simple architectures (one-hidden layer networks) and synthetic algebraic tasks.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more complex architectures and tasks.
Investigate margin maximization in more realistic settings.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations learned by neural networks is a cornerstone challenge in the science of machine learning. While there have been significant recent strides in some cases towards understanding how neural networks implement specific target functions, this paper explores a complementary question -- why do networks arrive at particular computational strategies? Our inquiry focuses on the algebraic learning tasks of modular addition, sparse parities, and finite group operations. Our primary theoretical findings analytically characterize the features learned by stylized neural networks for these algebraic tasks. Notably, our main technique demonstrates how the principle of margin maximization alone can be used to fully specify the features learned by the network. Specifically, we prove that the trained networks utilize Fourier features to perform modular addition and employ features corresponding to irreducible group-theoretic representations to perform compositions in general groups, aligning closely with the empirical observations of Nanda et al. and Chughtai et al. More generally, we hope our techniques can help to foster a deeper understanding of why neural networks adopt specific computational strategies.

papers.title: Evaluating Brain-Inspired Modular Training in Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does modular training (BIMT) affect the efficiency and quality of automated circuit discovery? How does modularity impact computational efficiency (training memory, time, inference)?
papers.core_contribution: Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT) significantly improves the efficiency and quality of automated circuit discovery, producing sparser circuits with lower logit differences and faster discovery times, though with increased training memory and time.
papers.conclusion: BIMT is an innovative and practical approach to neural network interpretability, enabling more efficient and effective circuit discovery, which is critical for analyzing large-scale models.
papers.key_findings:
BIMT achieves lower logit difference (1.2737 for circle detection) compared to other training regimes, indicating better circuit quality.
BIMT discovers circuits faster (93.76 seconds for circle detection) than other models.
BIMT produces sparser circuits (0.9859 sparsity for circle detection) which are easier to interpret.
BIMT requires more memory during training due to the swap operation, and has longer training times.
BIMT has slightly higher inference times compared to L1-only model (65.77 vs 64.65 seconds for 500000 images).
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to the MNIST dataset and MLP architecture, which may not generalize to other tasks and models.
Modular training may cause neurons to become polysemantic due to superposition, which could hinder interpretability.
future_direction: Test BIMT on transformer networks.
Investigate the effect of modularity on superposition.
Use attribution patching instead of activation patching for larger networks.
Evaluate BIMT on other tasks beyond digit classification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have experienced a rapid rise in AI, changing a wide range of applications with their advanced capabilities. As these models become increasingly integral to decision-making, the need for thorough interpretability has never been more critical. Mechanistic Interpretability offers a pathway to this understanding by identifying and analyzing specific sub-networks or 'circuits' within these complex systems. A crucial aspect of this approach is Automated Circuit Discovery, which facilitates the study of large models like GPT4 or LLAMA in a feasible manner. In this context, our research evaluates a recent method, Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT), designed to enhance the interpretability of neural networks. We demonstrate how BIMT significantly improves the efficiency and quality of Automated Circuit Discovery, overcoming the limitations of manual methods. Our comparative analysis further reveals that BIMT outperforms existing models in terms of circuit quality, discovery time, and sparsity. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive computational analysis of BIMT, including aspects such as training duration, memory allocation requirements, and inference speed. This study advances the larger objective of creating trustworthy and transparent AI systems in addition to demonstrating how well BIMT works to make neural networks easier to understand.

papers.title: The Distributed Information Bottleneck reveals the explanatory structure of complex systems
papers.research_question: How can we make deep learning interpretable for scientific discovery by decomposing complex relationships into a spectrum of meaningful approximations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Distributed Information Bottleneck, a framework that distributes bottlenecks across input components to decompose complex relationships into interpretable approximations, enabling analysis of information flow in deep learning models.
papers.conclusion: The Distributed Information Bottleneck brings interpretability to deep learning by providing a principled scheme of approximations that illuminates the explanatory structure of complex systems and enables unprecedented analysis of information flow.
papers.key_findings:
The Distributed IB can identify the most informative subsets of input components in a black-box Boolean circuit without exhaustive search.
Applied to the Mona Lisa, the Distributed IB produces a continuum of approximations that prioritize interactions between input components (e.g., horizontal and vertical axes) to reveal the relationship between position and color.
In a sheared glass system, the Distributed IB acts as a regularizer, prevents overfitting, and reveals that the relationship between static structure and imminent rearrangement is simpler in gradually quenched glasses than in rapidly quenched ones.
papers.abstract: The fruits of science are relationships made comprehensible, often by way of approximation. While deep learning is an extremely powerful way to find relationships in data, its use in science has been hindered by the difficulty of understanding the learned relationships. The Information Bottleneck (IB) is an information theoretic framework for understanding a relationship between an input and an output in terms of a trade-off between the fidelity and complexity of approximations to the relationship. Here we show that a crucial modification -- distributing bottlenecks across multiple components of the input -- opens fundamentally new avenues for interpretable deep learning in science. The Distributed Information Bottleneck throttles the downstream complexity of interactions between the components of the input, deconstructing a relationship into meaningful approximations found through deep learning without requiring custom-made datasets or neural network architectures. Applied to a complex system, the approximations illuminate aspects of the system's nature by restricting -- and monitoring -- the information about different components incorporated into the approximation. We demonstrate the Distributed IB's explanatory utility in systems drawn from applied mathematics and condensed matter physics. In the former, we deconstruct a Boolean circuit into approximations that isolate the most informative subsets of input components without requiring exhaustive search. In the latter, we localize information about future plastic rearrangement in the static structure of a sheared glass, and find the information to be more or less diffuse depending on the system's preparation. By way of a principled scheme of approximations, the Distributed IB brings much-needed interpretability to deep learning and enables unprecedented analysis of information flow through a system.

papers.title: Projective Kolmogorov Arnold Neural Networks (P-KANs): Entropy-Driven Functional Space Discovery for Interpretable Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we improve Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) by reducing redundancy in spline parameter spaces and guiding edge functions towards interpretable functional representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces P-KANs, a training framework that uses entropy-driven functional space projection to reduce parameter redundancy and improve interpretability in KANs.
papers.conclusion: P-KANs represent a step towards neural architectures that discover mathematical structure, improving parameter efficiency, noise robustness, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
P-KANs achieve up to 80% parameter reduction while maintaining representational capacity.
P-KANs show significantly improved robustness to noise compared to standard KANs.
P-KANs successfully apply to industrial automated fiber placement prediction with minimal data.
papers.limitation:
Computational overhead due to projection operations across multiple functional spaces.
Restriction to classical orthonormal bases may be insufficient for exotic phenomena.
Amplitude scaling issues may limit quantitative accuracy.
Hyperparameter sensitivity complicates deployment.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more general mathematical structures such as differential operators.
Hybrid deployment strategies to balance computational costs and robustness.
papers.abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) relocate learnable nonlinearities from nodes to edges, demonstrating remarkable capabilities in scientific machine learning and interpretable modeling. However, current KAN implementations suffer from fundamental inefficiencies due to redundancy in high-dimensional spline parameter spaces, where numerous distinct parameterisations yield functionally equivalent behaviors. This redundancy manifests as a "nuisance space" in the model's Jacobian, leading to susceptibility to overfitting and poor generalization. We introduce Projective Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (P-KANs), a novel training framework that guides edge function discovery towards interpretable functional representations through entropy-minimisation techniques from signal analysis and sparse dictionary learning. Rather than constraining functions to predetermined spaces, our approach maintains spline space flexibility while introducing "gravitational" terms that encourage convergence towards optimal functional representations. Our key insight recognizes that optimal representations can be identified through entropy analysis of projection coefficients, compressing edge functions to lower-parameter projective spaces (Fourier, Chebyshev, Bessel). P-KANs demonstrate superior performance across multiple domains, achieving up to 80% parameter reduction while maintaining representational capacity, significantly improved robustness to noise compared to standard KANs, and successful application to industrial automated fiber placement prediction. Our approach enables automatic discovery of mixed functional representations where different edges converge to different optimal spaces, providing both compression benefits and enhanced interpretability for scientific machine learning applications.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators: Model Recovery in Function Spaces
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be extended to operate in infinite-dimensional function spaces for concept learning, and what advantages do functional representations offer over standard SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse autoencoder neural operators (SAE-NOs) that operate in function spaces, specifically SAE-FNOs, which improve concept learning stability, robustness, and generalization compared to standard SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Functional representations in SAE-NOs extend sparse autoencoders from detectors of concept presence to models that capture the underlying structure of the data, highlighting parameterization as a central driver of interpretability and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-FNO successfully recovers ground-truth concepts in synthetic data and converges to zero dictionary recovery error.
SAE-FNO generalizes to unseen input resolutions, unlike SAE-CNN which fails beyond training resolution.
SAE-FNO learns concepts that are stable across different sparsity levels and exhibit diverse correlations, overcoming the orthogonality bias of SAE-MLP.
SAE-FNO achieves higher concept utilization efficiency, requiring fewer concepts to represent data, especially for larger domains.
Lifting accelerates concept recovery by acting as a preconditioner and improves optimization.
papers.abstract: We frame the problem of unifying representations in neural models as one of sparse model recovery and introduce a framework that extends sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to lifted spaces and infinite-dimensional function spaces, enabling mechanistic interpretability of large neural operators (NO). While the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that neural networks converge to similar representations across architectures, the representational properties of neural operators remain underexplored despite their growing importance in scientific computing. We compare the inference and training dynamics of SAEs, lifted-SAE, and SAE neural operators. We highlight how lifting and operator modules introduce beneficial inductive biases, enabling faster recovery, improved recovery of smooth concepts, and robust inference across varying resolutions, a property unique to neural operators.

papers.title: Insights Into the Inner Workings of Transformer Models for Protein Function Prediction
papers.research_question: How can explainable AI methods be extended to inspect latent representations in transformer models for protein function prediction, and do the identified relevant sequence parts reflect biological expectations?
papers.core_contribution: Extends integrated gradients to compute head-specific attributions in transformers for protein function prediction, showing that attribution maps correlate with biological sequence annotations and identifying specialized heads.
papers.conclusion: The extended integrated gradients method provides insights into transformer models for protein function prediction, showing that models focus on biologically relevant sequence parts and that specific heads are specialized for certain annotations.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution maps at the embedding layer correlate significantly with UniProt annotations for EC classes and GO membrane term.
Inside the model, specific transformer heads show significant correlation between attributions and annotations, indicating specialization.
For GO membrane term, heads with positive relevance and correlation with transmembrane regions are identified.
For GO catalytic activity, heads correlate with active sites and PROSITE patterns.
The method is sensitive to model parameters and provides insights beyond anecdotal evidence.
papers.limitation: The method may identify significant heads due to coincidental partial alignment of randomly initialized heads with directions in feature space that happen to correlate with sequence annotations.
papers.abstract: Motivation: We explored how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can help to shed light into the inner workings of neural networks for protein function prediction, by extending the widely used XAI method of integrated gradients such that latent representations inside of transformer models, which were finetuned to Gene Ontology term and Enzyme Commission number prediction, can be inspected too. Results: The approach enabled us to identify amino acids in the sequences that the transformers pay particular attention to, and to show that these relevant sequence parts reflect expectations from biology and chemistry, both in the embedding layer and inside of the model, where we identified transformer heads with a statistically significant correspondence of attribution maps with ground truth sequence annotations (e.g. transmembrane regions, active sites) across many proteins. Availability and Implementation: Source code can be accessed at https://github.com/markuswenzel/xai-proteins .

papers.title: Learning local discrete features in explainable-by-design convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design a convolutional neural network that is both high-performance and explainable by using a lateral inhibition mechanism to learn local discrete features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ExplaiNet, an explainable-by-design CNN that uses a lateral inhibition layer to learn local discrete feature vectors, enabling high accuracy and providing explanations via a probabilistic graph and motif discovery.
papers.conclusion: The ExplaiNet framework breaks the performance-explainability trade-off by introducing an explainable-by-design CNN that retains or surpasses baseline performance while providing causal explanations based on discrete feature motifs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed ExplaiNet model achieves comparable or better performance than baseline ResNet and DenseNet architectures on tiny image datasets while providing explanations.
The lateral inhibition layer amplifies gradients of winner neurons, leading to ordered activations and the formation of local discrete feature vectors.
Feature motif discovery using the EXTREME algorithm reduces the vocabulary of local discrete features, providing concise explanations.
The explainer probabilistic graph can infer causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs.
Experiments show that the explainer can sometimes correctly classify samples that the neural predictor misclassifies, suggesting potential for ensemble use or adversarial sample detection.
papers.limitation:
Further research on regularization aspects of the lateral inhibition function is required to investigate the magnitude of weights and activations during training.
Experiments are limited to tiny image datasets due to computational resources; the method has not been tested on medium-resolution images or high numbers of classes.
future_direction: Investigate the proper amount of weight decay and restriction of input values for positively monotonic gradient amplification in the lateral inhibition function.
Scale up the method to train models on medium-resolution images, high number of classes, and with millions of parameters.
Adjust the EXTREME algorithm to support custom numeric system bases, making the conversion to the quaternary system optional.
papers.abstract: Our proposed framework attempts to break the trade-off between performance and explainability by introducing an explainable-by-design convolutional neural network (CNN) based on the lateral inhibition mechanism. The ExplaiNet model consists of the predictor, that is a high-accuracy CNN with residual or dense skip connections, and the explainer probabilistic graph that expresses the spatial interactions of the network neurons. The value on each graph node is a local discrete feature (LDF) vector, a patch descriptor that represents the indices of antagonistic neurons ordered by the strength of their activations, which are learned with gradient descent. Using LDFs as sequences we can increase the conciseness of explanations by repurposing EXTREME, an EM-based sequence motif discovery method that is typically used in molecular biology. Having a discrete feature motif matrix for each one of intermediate image representations, instead of a continuous activation tensor, allows us to leverage the inherent explainability of Bayesian networks. By collecting observations and directly calculating probabilities, we can explain causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs. Moreover, experiments on various tiny image benchmark datasets confirm that our predictor ensures the same level of performance as the baseline architecture for a given count of parameters and/or layers. Our novel method shows promise to exceed this performance while providing an additional stream of explanations. In the solved MNIST classification task, it reaches a comparable to the state-of-the-art performance for single models, using standard training setup and 0.75 million parameters.

papers.title: Explaining the Explainer: Understanding the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Symbolic Regression Models
papers.research_question: How can we understand the internal mechanisms of transformer-based symbolic regression models, specifically by identifying circuits responsible for generating symbolic operators?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PATCHES, a novel evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm for symbolic regression transformers, and establishes a formal evaluation framework (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) for circuit correctness.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes symbolic regression as a promising domain for mechanistic interpretability and provides a principled methodology for circuit discovery in such models.
papers.key_findings:
PATCHES successfully isolates circuits for specific symbolic operators (e.g., sin, add, log) in a transformer-based SR model.
Mean patching combined with functional evaluation (accuracy) is more reliable for discovering correct circuits than resample patching or model-based (logit) evaluation.
Direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features, limiting their utility for causal circuit discovery.
Circuits for SR are dense (40-78% of model components), attributed to the small vocabulary and complex syntactic encoding required.
papers.limitation:
Resample patching sometimes fails to sufficiently suppress the target token's information, hindering causal isolation and circuit discovery.
High baseline performance for some operators (e.g., addition) makes it difficult to achieve completeness, as patching does not degrade performance enough.
papers.abstract: Following their success across many domains, transformers have also proven effective for symbolic regression (SR); however, the internal mechanisms underlying their generation of mathematical operators remain largely unexplored. Although mechanistic interpretability has successfully identified circuits in language and vision models, it has not yet been applied to SR. In this article, we introduce PATCHES, an evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm that identifies compact and correct circuits for SR. Using PATCHES, we isolate 28 circuits, providing the first circuit-level characterisation of an SR transformer. We validate these findings through a robust causal evaluation framework based on key notions such as faithfulness, completeness, and minimality. Our analysis shows that mean patching with performance-based evaluation most reliably isolates functionally correct circuits. In contrast, we demonstrate that direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features rather than causal ones, limiting their utility for circuit discovery. Overall, these results establish SR as a high-potential application domain for mechanistic interpretability and propose a principled methodology for circuit discovery.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Hierarchical Sparse Circuit Extraction from Billion-Parameter Language Models through Scalable Attribution Graph Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can sparse computational circuits be efficiently extracted from billion-parameter language models using hierarchical decomposition and attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD), a framework that reduces circuit discovery complexity from exponential to polynomial, enabling extraction of interpretable circuits from billion-parameter models with high behavioral preservation.
papers.conclusion: HAGD enables circuit extraction from large models with preserved behavior, but limitations include incomplete attention modeling, reconstruction residuals, and interpretability challenges for large circuits.
papers.key_findings:
HAGD reduces circuit discovery complexity to O(n^2 log n) and extracts circuits from models up to 70B parameters.
Behavioral preservation ranges from 82% to 97% on algorithmic tasks and 74% to 88% on natural language benchmarks.
Cross-architecture transfer shows 52%-82% structural similarity, indicating shared computational patterns.
Circuit size grows sublinearly with model parameters, but natural language tasks yield larger, less modular circuits.
The method outperforms baselines like ACDC in scalability while maintaining comparable circuit quality.
papers.limitation:
Attention circuits are not modeled, leaving significant computational pathways unanalyzed.
Reconstruction dark matter of 15-20% unexplained variance means extracted circuits are incomplete.
Validation circularity arises from using ablation experiments that assume circuit completeness.
GNN meta-model requires ground-truth circuit labels that are expensive to obtain.
Large circuits with hundreds of nodes may exceed human interpretability limits.
future_direction: Integrate attention and MLP circuit analysis.
Characterize reconstruction residuals (dark matter).
Develop label-efficient training methods for GNN meta-model.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural network computations into human-understandable algorithms, yet extracting sparse computational circuits from billion-parameter language models remains challenging due to exponential search complexity and pervasive polysemanticity. The proposed Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD) framework reduces circuit discovery complexity from O(2^n) exhaustive enumeration to O(n^2 log n) through multi-resolution abstraction hierarchies and differentiable circuit search. The methodology integrates cross-layer transcoders for monosemantic feature extraction, graph neural network meta-learning for topology prediction, and causal intervention protocols for validation. Empirical evaluation spans GPT-2 variants, Llama-7B through Llama-70B, and Pythia suite models across algorithmic tasks and natural language benchmarks. On modular arithmetic tasks, the framework achieves up to 91% behavioral preservation ($\pm$2.3\% across runs) while maintaining interpretable subgraph sizes. Cross-architecture transfer experiments suggest that discovered circuits exhibit moderate structural similarity (averaging 67%) across model families, indicating potential shared computational patterns. These results provide preliminary foundations for interpretability at larger model scales while identifying significant limitations in current attribution methodologies that require future advances.

papers.title: Deep learning and density-functional theory
papers.abstract: We show that deep neural networks can be integrated into, or fully replace, the Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) scheme for multielectron systems in simple harmonic oscillator and random external potentials with no feature engineering. We first show that self-consistent charge densities calculated with different exchange-correlation functionals can be used as input to an extensive deep neural network to make predictions for correlation, exchange, external, kinetic, and total energies simultaneously. Additionally, we show that one can make all of the same predictions with the external potential rather than the self-consistent charge density, which allows one to circumvent the Kohn-Sham DFT scheme altogether. We then show that a self-consistent charge density found from a nonlocal exchange-correlation functional can be used to make energy predictions for a semilocal exchange-correlation functional. Lastly, we use a deep convolutional inverse graphics network to predict the charge density given an external potential for different exchange-correlation functionals and assess the viability of the predicted charge densities. This work shows that extensive deep neural networks are generalizable and transferable given the variability of the potentials (maximum total energy range $\ensuremath{\approx}100$ Ha) because they require no feature engineering and because they can scale to an arbitrary system size with an $O(N)$ computational cost.

papers.title: Improving density matrix electronic structure method by deep learning
papers.abstract: The combination of deep learning and ab initio materials calculations is emerging as a trending frontier of materials science research, with deep-learning density functional theory (DFT) electronic structure being particularly promising. In this work, we introduce a neural-network method for modeling the DFT density matrix, a fundamental yet previously unexplored quantity in deep-learning electronic structure. Utilizing an advanced neural network framework that leverages the nearsightedness and equivariance properties of the density matrix, the method demonstrates high accuracy and excellent generalizability in multiple example studies, as well as capability to precisely predict charge density and reproduce other electronic structure properties. Given the pivotal role of the density matrix in DFT as well as other computational methods, the current research introduces a novel approach to the deep-learning study of electronic structure properties, opening up new opportunities for deep-learning enhanced computational materials study.

papers.title: Learning the Exchange-Correlation Functional from Nature with Fully Differentiable Density Functional Theory
papers.abstract: Improving the predictive capability of molecular properties in ab initio simulations is essential for advanced material discovery. Despite recent progress making use of machine learning, utilizing deep neural networks to improve quantum chemistry modeling remains severely limited by the scarcity and heterogeneity of appropriate experimental data. Here we show how training a neural network to replace the exchange-correlation functional within a fully differentiable three-dimensional Kohn-Sham density functional theory framework can greatly improve simulation accuracy. Using only eight experimental data points on diatomic molecules, our trained exchange-correlation networks enable improved prediction accuracy of atomization energies across a collection of 104 molecules containing new bonds, and atoms, that are not present in the training dataset.

papers.title: Machine-learning-based exchange correlation functional with physical asymptotic constraints
papers.abstract: Density functional theory is the standard theory for computing the electronic structure of materials, which is based on a functional that maps the electron density to the energy. However, a rigorous form of the functional is not known and has been heuristically constructed by interpolating asymptotic constraints known for extreme situations, such as isolated atoms and uniform electron gas. Recent studies have demonstrated that the functional can be effectively approximated using machine learning (ML) approaches. However, most ML models do not satisfy asymptotic constraints. In this paper, by applying a ML model architecture, we demonstrate a neural network-based exchange-correlation functional satisfying physical asymptotic constraints. Calculations reveal that the trained functional is applicable to various materials with an accuracy higher than that of existing functionals, even for materials whose electronic properties are not included in training dataset. Our proposed method thus improves the accuracy and generalization performance of the ML-based functional by combining the advantages of ML and analytical modeling.

papers.title: Deep Charge: A Deep Learning Model of Electron Density from One-Shot Density Functional Theory Calculation
papers.abstract: Electron charge density is a fundamental physical quantity, determining various properties of matter. In this study, we have proposed a deep-learning model for accurate charge density prediction. Our model naturally preserves physical symmetries and can be effectively trained from one-shot density functional theory calculation toward high accuracy. It captures detailed atomic environment information, ensuring accurate predictions of charge density across bulk, surface, molecules, and amorphous structures. This implementation exhibits excellent scalability and provides efficient analyses of material properties in large-scale condensed matter systems.

papers.title: Deep Neural Network Computes Electron Densities and Energies of a Large Set of Organic Molecules Faster than Density Functional Theory (DFT)
papers.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) is one of the main methods in Quantum Chemistry that offers an attractive trade off between the cost and accuracy of quantum chemical computations. The electron density plays a key role in DFT. In this work, we explore whether machine learning - more specifically, deep neural networks (DNNs) - can be trained to predict electron densities faster than DFT. First, we choose a practically efficient combination of a DFT functional and a basis set (PBE0/pcS-3) and use it to generate a database of DFT solutions for more than 133,000 organic molecules from a previously published database QM9. Next, we train a DNN to predict electron densities and energies of such molecules. The only input to the DNN is an approximate electron density computed with a cheap quantum chemical method in a small basis set (HF/cc-VDZ). We demonstrate that the DNN successfully learns differences in the electron densities arising both from electron correlation and small basis set artifacts in the HF computations. All qualitative features in density differences, including local minima on lone pairs, local maxima on nuclei, toroidal shapes around C-H and C-C bonds, complex shapes around aromatic and cyclopropane rings and CN group, etc. are captured by the DNN. Accuracy of energy predictions by the DNN is ~ 1 kcal/mol, on par with other models reported in the literature, while those models do not predict the electron density. Computations with the DNN, including HF computations, take much less time that DFT computations (by a factor of ~20-30 for most QM9 molecules in the current version, and it is clear how it could be further improved).

papers.title: DeepDFT: Neural Message Passing Network for Accurate Charge Density Prediction
papers.abstract: We introduce DeepDFT, a deep learning model for predicting the electronic charge density around atoms, the fundamental variable in electronic structure simulations from which all ground state properties can be calculated. The model is formulated as neural message passing on a graph, consisting of interacting atom vertices and special query point vertices for which the charge density is predicted. The accuracy and scalability of the model are demonstrated for molecules, solids and liquids. The trained model achieves lower average prediction errors than the observed variations in charge density obtained from density functional theory simulations using different exchange correlation functionals.

papers.title: NeuralSCF: Neural network self-consistent fields for density functional theory
papers.abstract: Kohn-Sham density functional theory (KS-DFT) has found widespread application in accurate electronic structure calculations.
